catalog_quote: Accentuation et intonation. — L'accent tonique n'existe pas en dahoméen et ceci s'explique facilement. Les mots n'étant que des radicaux juxtaposés, sans terminaisons formatives, chacune des syllabes a autant d'importance que les autres et on ne peut pas faire ressortir l'une d'elle aux dépens de ses voisines. Il faut donc prononcer recto tono toutes les syllabes d'un mot. Mais si l'accentuation proprement dite fait défaut, on rencontre en revanche l'intonation propre à un grand nombre de parlers nègres et qui se fait sentir, non sur les mots, mais sur les phrases. Chez les Dahoméens elle présente deux caractères principaux : le plus général est un arrêt brusque de la voix sur la dernière syllabe de la phrase, ou sur la dernière syllabe du mot important, ce qui précède ayant été débité avec volubilité et sur le même ton; le second caractère consiste dans un redoublement des consonnes in…
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Fon (fonn1241) is not in the catalog. The only title-keyword item, Gbéto 2004 (JWAL 31(1): 15-31), was already held by the project and was read in full: it is about prosodic-word minimality in French loans, treats Fon as a two-toneme /H, L/ language, and uses 'syllabe accentuée' only for the French source syllable that Fon maps to H tone (pp. 17, 23-24, 26); it says nothing about native Fon word stress, so relevance = prosody-but-not-word-stress, priority none. The JWAL landing page was re-checked (Volume 31, No. 1, PDF 140.34 KB = on-disk file). The best first-hand stress statement read is Delafosse 1894 Manuel dahoméen p. 36 (held by the project): 'L'accent tonique n'existe pas en dahoméen.. prononcer recto tono toutes les syllabes d'un mot' — Fon has no word stress. No new files downloaded

new_statements.translation: Accentuation and intonation. — Tonic (word) stress does not exist in Dahomean, and this is easily explained. Since words are merely juxtaposed roots without formative endings, each syllable has as much importance as the others and one cannot make one of them stand out at the expense of its neighbours. One must therefore pronounce all the syllables of a word evenly (recto tono). But if accentuation proper is lacking, one finds instead the intonation ... which makes itself felt not on words but on phrases. Among the Dahomeans ... the most general feature is an abrupt stop of the voice on the last syllable of the phrase, or on the last syllable of the important word

new_statements.rule_in_words: No word-level stress: all syllables of a word are equally prominent; prominence phenomena are phrase-level only (abrupt arrest of the voice on the phrase-final syllable or on the final syllable of the focal word; emphatic gemination of a word-initial consonant). Modern descriptions instead analyse Fon as a two-toneme (H/L) language and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None for words; phrase-final syllable / final syllable of the 'important word' receives an abrupt arrest of the voice (phrase-level, not lexical). Delafosse does not recognise lexical tone at all, so his 'no accent' claim is a 19th-century impressionistic statement.
new_statements.domain_note: Explicitly distinguishes word level (no accent) from phrase level (intonational prominence at phrase end). Variety: 'dahoméen' = Fon of the Abomey kingdom/Ouidah coast as heard by Delafosse in 1890s. Contrast: Henrici 1891 p. 18 claims for Ewe ('Ephe') generally that the last syllable of polysyllables usually carries the 'Wortton'; modern Fon sources opened (Gbéto 2004, Höftmann & Ahohounkpanzon 2003 esquisse, Gnanguenon 2014, Laleye 2016) describe two tonemes H/L and are silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Delafosse 1894 describes 'la langue dahoméenne' = Fon (fɔ̀ngbè) of the Abomey kingdom and the Ouidah/Cotonou coast, i.e. fonn1241 proper (he explicitly distinguishes it from Anlo Ewe and 'Mina'/Gen). Gbéto 2004 describes the Cotonou variety of Fon. Henrici 1891's word-accent remark is for Ewe ('Ephe', ewee1241 sensu lato, Anlo-based) with Fon treated as the 'Dahome-Mundart', so it should not be attributed to fonn1241 on its own.

new_statements.translation: Accentuation and intonation. — Word stress (l'accent tonique) does not exist in Dahomean, and this is easily explained. Since words are merely juxtaposed roots without formative endings, each syllable has as much weight as the others and none can be made prominent at the expense of its neighbours. All the syllables of a word must therefore be pronounced recto tono. But if accentuation proper is lacking, one finds instead the intonation typical of many African languages, which is felt not on words but on phrases.
new_statements.citation: Delafosse, Maurice. 1894. Manuel dahoméen: grammaire, chrestomathie, dictionnaire français-dahoméen et dahoméen-français. Paris: Ernest Leroux.
new_statements.locator: p. 36, section 'Accentuation et intonation' (PDF page 48 of the archive.org scan)
new_statements.reading: First-hand 19th-century statement that Fon (Dahomean = Fongbe of Dahomey) has no word stress; every syllable of a word is equally prominent. Consistent with the modern description (Gbéto 2004 sec. 2.3, held by the project) of Fon as a two-toneme /H, L/ language in which the stress of French loan sources is converted to H tone. If Fon were catalogued, the classification would be 'no word stress / lexical tone'. This file was already held by the project from an earlier reading today; nothing new was downloaded in this search of works with stress in the title.

sources.locator: p. 36, section 'Accentuation et intonation' (Première partie, phonétique); = PDF page 48 of the archive.org scan manueldahomengr00delagoog
sources.note: p. 36 'Accentuation et intonation': explicit statement that 'l'accent tonique n'existe pas en dahoméen'; all syllables of a word pronounced evenly ('recto tono'); instead there is phrase-level intonation: an abrupt stop of the voice on the last syllable of the phrase or of the important word, and emphatic doubling of initial consonants. (Pre-tonal-analysis description: lexical tone is not recognised.)

sources.citation: Henrici, Ernst. 1891. Lehrbuch der Ephe-Sprache (Ewe): Anlo-, Anecho- und Dahome-Mundart, mit Glossar und einer Karte der Sklavenküste. Stuttgart/Berlin: W. Spemann.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p. 18 'Wort- und Satzbetonung, Intonation': 'Bei mehrsilbigen Wörtern hat die letzte Silbe in der Regel den Wortton' (in polysyllabic words the last syllable as a rule carries the word accent), followed by three 'Tonstufen' (Hochton, Tiefton, Tonlosigkeit) that distinguish word meanings. Stated for 'Ephe' (Ewe) as a whole on an Anlo basis; the Dahome (Fongbe) section pp. 165ff only says the Anecho pronunciation rules also hold for Dahome. Old, Ewe-wide, and at odds with Delafosse.

sources.citation: Gbéto, Flavien. 2004. L'expression de la minimalité prosodique dans les emprunts européens en fon. Journal of West African Languages 31(1): 15-31. (Glottolog id 163020 gives pp. 15-32.)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: p. 17: "Au niveau phonétique, le fon présente les tons suivants: B, H, M, B-H, H-B, B-H-B. De ces réalisations tonales, seules B et H ont statut de phonèmes". p. 23: "les formes adaptées (voir Gbéto 2000a) se voient assignées la structure (B) H B. Dans cette formule, la syllabe accentuée est préassociée avec le ton H, le ton B final désigne la pause ou la descente de la voix observée en position finale et le ton B initial (facultatif, si le mot ne commence pas par une syllabe non accentuée) représente l'interprétation des syllabes inaccentuées." p. 26: "puisque tout mot emprunté doit comporter une syllabe accentuée, on comprend la structure tonale /H B/: le premier ton H est l'interprétation de phénomènes accentuels"
sources.locator: sec. 2.3 p. 17 (tone system); pp. 23-24 (tone melody assigned to adapted French loans); p. 26 (loan verbs)
sources.note: The paper is about prosodic-word minimality (max three tonal units) in French loans and reduplicated verbs. 'Syllabe accentuée' throughout refers to the stressed syllable of the FRENCH source form, which Fon re-interprets as H tone (melody (B) H B for adapted loans, B H for truncated forms). Fon itself is described as a two-toneme language (/B/, /H/); the paper makes no statement about native Fon word stress or any stress placement rule in Fon. sources.citation: Wekenon Tokponto, Mensah (2002). Deutsch-beninische Märchenforschung am Beispiel von Märchen in der Fon-Sprache mit phonetischer Transkription, Studie und Darstellung der Hauptfiguren und Themenvergleich. Univ. University of Bielefeld. 298 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Says nothing about stress, so it neither confirms nor contradicts Delafosse 1894 ('L'accent tonique n'existe pas en dahoméen'); its tonal description (lexical + grammatical tone on every syllable) is compatible with the existing statements and with Gbéto 2004's two-toneme analysis, though it lists five surface tones (H, L, LH, HL, M) where Gbéto posits two tonemes. The phonetics sketch is explicitly a brief practical orientation for the folktale transcriptions, not a phonological analysis, and it leans on Höftmann's Grammatik des Fon.
